# I built a side project to test TypeSafe's Jev model with no generative LLM that scores your project idea
TypeSafe released the Jev model, and to test it, I built this small project where you enter your idea and the system gives you a score through around 10 questions and classifications, all run in parallel. That’s the magic of Jev.

The project is open source because it’s purely demonstrative, but I think it can still be useful for quickly validating an idea.

A project like this would previously have required 30-60 seconds of reasoning from an LLM, with several different evaluations. Jev, instead, runs all the requests in parallel and returns a score.

## PrizeSyntax
### stemonte
It's incredibly useful for categorization, if we want to simplify. In my linked tool, I input the idea and 10 questions, and it evaluates those 10 questions, which the tool then uses to classify your idea.

## blu3n0va
### stemonte
At the moment, under the hood, it uses JEV. Basically, I take the idea and the goal and pass them to JEV with a series of questions (and choices) to which it responds with a score. Then the app takes the score for each item and comes up with an overall value. It's very basic, but it's a sensible use case for testing JEV, which is strong in categorization.
You can take a look at the "questions" asked to JEV to evaluate the idea here: https://github.com/monteduro/killmyidea/blob/main/src/lib/questions.ts

## Fohawkkid
### stemonte
The output is generated by a model named Jev (typesafe.ai). It's like asking ChatGPT, but it works completely differently. Based on certain questions asked about an input (your idea), it gives you a score for each of the 10 questions. Then, based on the score, my app presents you with outputs.

## impartingboss
### AllOverTheWorld › impartingboss › stemonte
It's definitely not a wrapper since it accepts input text (of any kind) and always outputs judgment values, so to speak. In the case of my KillMyIdea, I pass the idea with about 10 questions to which it provides validation. It does this in parallel, so it really takes just fractions of a second.

## comment
### stemonte

Well, for a few pretty obvious reasons: it processes requests in parallel. In my tool, I send it 10 scoring questions and it handles them simultaneously in under 600ms.

 It costs next to nothing and the output is minimal because it only returns JSON or single values.

# Jev returns a typed decision plus a probability instead of text. Where that actually fits in an agent pipeline.
TypeSafe AI shipped a model called Jev last week. It is not another chat model, and the shape is relevant to anyone building agents, so here is a breakdown of where it slots in and where it does not.

You send program state plus a set of typed questions. It returns typed answers with a probability distribution on each, in one parallel pass. No text generation at all. Three primitives:

Context is 64K per request, 32K of that for state plus the longest single question. Text only. Input runs $0.042 per million tokens, output is free.

The obvious slots are the decision points you currently implement as a small LLM call wrapped in JSON parsing and a retry:

* Routing: which tool, which sub-agent, which queue

The useful part is not the speed, it is that every answer carries a probability. You can set an explicit confidence threshold per decision point and route anything below it to a stronger model or a human, instead of discovering later that your classifier was confidently wrong.

TypeSafe publishes a model jaggedness page that is unusually candid about failure modes. Jev does not count reliably. It underperforms on numeric formats like hex or RGB. It cannot reliably judge whether two values are near each other. It reads dates as text rather than as ordered quantities. Accuracy degrades as state grows with content unrelated to the decision, which matters a lot if you are dumping a whole agent trace into it. Multi-hop questions and double negatives degrade too, so decompose them.

## jonah_omninode
The architectural boundary I would emphasize is that a typed result is executable, but it is not automatically correct. The runtime still needs to own permissions, state transitions, and verification.

 JEV can choose among allowed next actions and attach probabilities. Code should decide whether the confidence is sufficient, execute the action, and record whether the outcome actually passed.
